title: Introduction to hvtiBoostmtree
text: boostmtree extends Friedman’s (2001) gradient descent boosting framework handle longitudinal response data using multivariate tree base learners penalized B-splines (P-splines) model covariate–time interactions. package supports four response families: Although package designed longitudinal data, degrades gracefully standard boosting model subject single observation.

title: Introduction to hvtiBoostmtree
text: simLong() generates synthetic longitudinal datasets varying degrees covariate–time interaction complexity. Four simulation models provided:
code:
library(hvtiBoostmtree)  set.seed(42) dta <- simLong(   n      = 50,     # training subjects   ntest  = 25,     # test subjects   N      = 5,      # average ~5 time points per subject   model  = 1,      # linear time × x2 interaction   family = "Continuous",   q      = 3       # 3 noise variables added )  ## Data is returned in two formats ## dta$dta   — flat data.frame ## dta$dtaL  — list with $features, $time, $id, $y  cat("Training rows:", sum(dta$dtaL$id %in% unique(dta$dtaL$id)[dta$trn]), "
") #> Training rows: 682 cat("True model:   ", dta$f.true, "
") #> True model:    y ~ g( x1 + x3 + x4 + I(time * x2) ) cat("Covariates:   ", ncol(dta$dtaL$features), "
") #> Covariates:    7

text: main entry point boostmtree(). Key tuning parameters : cv.flag = TRUE option uses --bag samples iteration select optimal stopping point Mopt, protecting overfitting without separate held-validation set.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis with hvtiBoostmtree
text: Standard regression methods struggle longitudinal data: repeated measures correlated within subjects, observation schedules often unbalanced, covariate effects can change time. boostmtree handles three combining multivariate tree base learners (non-linear covariate effects) adaptive P-splines (covariate–time interactions), without requiring imputation balanced panel. vignette demonstrates full analysis workflow using two bundled real datasets.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis with hvtiBoostmtree
text: spirometry dataset contains 9,471 post-lung-transplant FEV1% measurements 509 patients along 23 baseline clinical covariates. boostmtree() expects data long format (one row per observation), split four components: code shows full production fit (M = 200, cv.flag = TRUE). keep vignette build time short, pre-computed results loaded package’s inst/extdata/ directory available. top-left panel shows OOB error (RMSE) vs. boosting iteration. dashed vertical line marks selected Mopt. text: simLong() supports systematic benchmarking across simulation models. compare OOB RMSE across four simulation scenarios continuous response. expected, error increases model complexity (richer covariate–time interactions), boosting adapts Mopt accordingly.
code: results <- lapply(0:3, function(m) {   set.seed(m + 100)   dta <- simLong(n = 50, ntest = 0, N = 4, model = m,                  family = "Continuous", q = 2)   fit <- boostmtree(     x       = dta$dtaL$features,     tm      = dta$dtaL$time,     id      = dta$dtaL$id,     y       = dta$dtaL$y,     family  = "Continuous",     M       = 50,     cv.flag = TRUE,     verbose = FALSE   )   data.frame(     model    = paste0("Model ", m),     formula  = dta$f.true,     Mopt     = fit$Mopt[1],     OOB_RMSE = round(min(fit$rmse, na.rm = TRUE), 3)   ) })  do.call(rbind, results) #>     model                                            formula Mopt OOB_RMSE #> 1 Model 0                              y ~ g( x1 + x3 + x4 )   50    0.918 #> 2 Model 1               y ~ g( x1 + x3 + x4 + I(time * x2) )   50    0.680 #> 3 Model 2           y ~ g( x1 + x3 + x4 + I(time^2 * x2^2) )   50    0.611 #> 4 Model 3 y ~ g( x1 + x3 + exp(x4) + I(time^2 * x2^2 * x3) )   50    0.597
